Below is a strengthened, evidence-backed set of references and rationale to modernize and contextualize your proposal on molecular characterization of malaria vectors across agricultural and residential land-use types in Western North Region, Ghana, with implications for targeted control.

Why precision surveillance now
- Malaria remains a leading cause of outpatient visits and contributes to high annual burdens in Ghana, with peaks during rainy seasons; urban and peri-urban settings face persistent transmission driven by anthropogenic and agricultural land-use changes that create larval habitats and alter adult mosquito behavior and exposure opportunities. <cite id="45dcaaa6-0">In Ghana’s forest–savanna transition and middle belt, bimodal rainfall and warm temperatures foster breeding, with An. gambiae, An. arabiensis, and An. funestus predominating</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-0">Abundant vegetation, rivers and streams, and a forest–savanna mosaic create convenient breeding conditions and elevate transmission</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-0">Predominant vectors include An. gambiae, An. arabiensis, and An. funestus</cite>. 
- Transmission is intensely heterogeneous even among proximate villages, varying with land cover, proximity to breeding sites, agriculture, and house design; these microgeographies are essential targets for precision interventions. <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Annual biting rates and EIR ranged from 371–1890 and 40–158 across four forest-zone villages; ABR strongly predicted parasite density</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Malaria transmission was intense and heterogeneous, corresponding to micro-ecological differences</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Infectious mosquitoes persisted year-round except in dry months; spring-fed habitats sustained perennial transmission</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Proximity to plantain/banana plantations was associated with higher incidence; leaf axils serve as larval microhabitats</cite>. 
- Agricultural intensification and urbanization reshape breeding landscapes: irrigated urban farming and peri-urban sites harbor abundant larval habitats (drainage ditches, puddles, tyres), and human-altered land-use drives vector proliferation. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Urban breeding habitats included drainage ditches, car tyres, puddles; irrigated urban farming and peri-urban sites had the highest frequency of larval habitats</cite> <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Drainage ditches were most abundant and productive; An. coluzzii predominated; An. stephensi was first detected in Accra</cite> <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Most habitats were anthropogenic, reflecting urbanization and agriculture; land-use shapes breeding habitats</cite>. 
- Entomological surveillance and integration with epidemiology are now central to last‑mile elimination strategies, especially to detect active foci and guide evidence-based vector control. <cite id="21998773-0">Routine entomological surveillance in high-transmission and elimination foci is emphasized; combining mosquito data with epidemiology supports operational decisions</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Vectors were highly anthropophilic with nocturnal biting peaks; 17% collected indoors and 32% outdoors; residual transmission occurs outdoors in cultivation fields and forested areas</cite>. 
- National and global programmes underscore the need for robust vector surveillance systems and spatial targeting; weak capacity to implement vector surveillance is common, highlighting the opportunity and necessity for active, precision surveillance. <cite id="21998773-2">Only 8% of NMCPs reported sufficient capacity to implement vector surveillance; capacity gaps in strategic planning, training, logistics underpin weak surveillance</cite> <cite id="21998773-4">High-quality surveillance data are central to the Global Technical Strategy; Ghana’s plan aims for large morbidity/mortality reductions with surveillance to inform control</cite>.

Current vector ecology and land-use linkages in Ghana relevant to Western North
- Species composition and distribution: An. gambiae s.l. predominates across ecological zones with An. coluzzii and An. gambiae s.s. frequently dominant; sporozoite infection rates and human blood feeding are higher in forest and Sahel savanna than coastal sites. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Anopheles gambiae s.l., particularly An. coluzzii and An. gambiae s.s., were predominant across 12 sites in Coastal, Forest and Sahel zones</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Sporozoite infections were higher in forest and Sahel than coastal; overall human blood index 40.46%</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">EIR and infection data support spatial targeting across ecological zones</cite>. 
- Molecular forms and control: Distribution of M/S forms and insecticide resistance patterns underpin intervention choice; national policy prioritizes LLINs and IRS, but their efficiency depends on accurate vector distribution and molecular forms. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">An. gambiae s.l. contains species including An. gambiae s.s., An. arabiensis, and An. melas; major malaria vectors in West Africa</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana’s policy prioritizes LLINs and IRS; efficiency depends on distribution, abundance, molecular forms, and resistance</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Baseline surveys on An. gambiae s.s. distribution and resistance are needed; S form predominates countrywide, M form in arid north</cite>. 
- Western North context: The region sits in a forest–savanna mosaic with cocoa and other agriculture, a setting analogous to Ghana’s transitional zones where land-use change, irrigation, and vegetation structure create heterogeneous larval habitats and exposure. <cite id="45dcaaa6-0">The middle belt and forest–savanna mosaic with rivers and streams fosters breeding</cite> <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated urban farming and peri-urban sites harbor abundant larval habitats; drainage ditches are highly productive</cite>. 
- Agricultural practices introduce additional larval sources and outdoor biting exposure: cultivation fields, drainage near farms, and irrigation infrastructure provide persistent water and organic inputs, sustaining vector populations and outdoor transmission. <cite id="21998773-0">Residual transmission occurs outdoors in cultivation fields and forested areas</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-2">Agricultural insecticides used in crop protection risk resistance and may interfere with malaria vector control, complicating insecticide management</cite>.

Molecular and entomological methods for precise mapping
- Species delineation and biodiversity: Recent reclassification of An. gambiae complex molecular forms into An. coluzzii (M) and An. gambiae (S) motivates species-specific analyses and habitat preference studies; cryptic diversity requires molecular markers to guide control and resistance monitoring. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-0">Following reclassification of M and S forms into An. coluzzii and An. gambiae s.s., habitat preferences in urban settings were reassessed</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Distribution and molecular forms (M/S) are key determinants of vector control efficiency and resistance monitoring</cite>. 
- Recommended PCR-based vector ID: Use of molecular species identification (e.g., COI barcoding and species replacement diagnostic regions such as SRD/SPMS) resolves An. gambiae s.l. into S/coluzzii and gambiae s.s., and detects hybrids; this has been validated across Ghana and supports hotspot detection. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Morphological and molecular ID combined with blood-meal PCR provide robust vector profiles across ecological zones</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Molecular forms and resistance inform intervention selection; baseline surveys and ID are needed where reliable data are lacking</cite>. 
- Plasmodium detection and EIR integration: Species-specific Plasmodium detection using 18S rRNA primers and quantification (qPCR) yields sensitive estimates of infection rates and parasite species; combined with mosquito species and host blood-meal data, EIR can be estimated at fine spatial scales. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Sporozoite infection rates assessed by PCR across ecological zones inform EIR and risk mapping</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">EIR and ABR measured via human landing catches and sporozoite ELISA/PCR underpin spatial risk inference</cite>. 
- Geospatial integration: Overlaying EIR with land-use/land-cover, irrigation, and agriculture layers identifies agricultural and peri-urban vector hotspots and explains cross-site heterogeneity, aligning with surveillance strategies for elimination. <cite id="21998773-0">Linking entomological and epidemiological data with spatial context supports operational decision-making in elimination</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Micro-ecological features drive ABR/EIR variation; scaling preventive measures reduces exposure and parasitemia</cite>.

Expected spatial patterns across cocoa/agricultural vs. residential/peri-urban sites
- Agricultural interfaces: Irrigated and non-irrigated crop lands (cocoa, plantains/bananas) create numerous artificial and semi-natural larval habitats (ditches, field edge pools, tyre/utensil collections, puddles), attract high densities of An. gambiae s.l., and sustain outdoor biting and sporozoite-positive outdoor collection. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated urban farming and peri-urban sites had the highest frequency of larval habitats; drainage ditches most productive</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor and residual transmission occurs in cultivation fields; 32% of vectors collected outdoors at times people are awake</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Proximity to plantain/banana plantations associated with higher incidence; leaf axils harbor larvae</cite>. 
- Residential/peri-urban interfaces: House eaves, refuse, drainage, and anthropogenic containers amplify breeding; An. coluzzii predominance and anthropophilic, endophilic biting elevate indoor infection risk and EIR near residential clusters, especially after heavy rains. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">An. coluzzii dominated in urban habitats; most breeding sites anthropogenic; drainage ditches linked to domestic effluents</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Human blood index ~40% and higher sporozoite rates in forest/savanna zones suggest elevated indoor infection risk where domestic breeding occurs</cite>. 
- Forest–savanna mosaics: Vegetation complexity increases larval refuge and adult resting sites; edge effects and spring-fed wetlands maintain year-round breeding, sustaining high EIR and perennial transmission risk. <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Spring-fed habitats sustained perennial breeding and transmission; infectious mosquitoes persisted outside dry season</cite>.

Implications for targeted control strategies
- Spatial targeting of LLINs and IRS: Sites with high EIR and anthropophilic, endophilic biting should receive priority LLIN distribution and, where feasible, focal IRS; outdoor exposure calls for additional personal protection and community-level interventions. <cite id="21998773-0">Indoors account for 17% of collection; 32% outdoors at times people are awake, underscoring need for nets and personal protection</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Residual transmission outdoors in cultivation and forests necessitates spatially targeted control beyond indoor measures</cite>. 
- Larval source management (LSM) on farms: Drainage modification, container elimination, biological control (larvivorous fish), and targeted larviciding in irrigation channels and crop-associated depressions can substantially reduce larval indices; evidence from urban/peri-urban Ghana shows irrigation farming and peri-urban interfaces as LSM hotspots. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated urban farming had highest larval habitat frequency; drainage ditches highly productive—targets for LSM</cite> <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Most habitats anthropogenic; land-use management reduces breeding</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-2">Agricultural insecticides risk resistance; integrated vector management is needed, separating crop protection from public health insecticides</cite>. 
- Insecticide resistance and co-management: Agricultural insecticide use selects resistance; integrated surveillance of An. gambiae s.l. and resistance in Western North will inform safer combinations (e.g., botanical/pyrethroid rotations) and non-chemical tools. <cite id="45dcaaa6-2">Continuous agricultural insecticide utilization poses resistance risk to malaria vector control</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Efficiency of LLINs/IRS depends on molecular forms and resistance levels—baseline surveys and monitoring are essential</cite>. 
- Precision surveillance framework: Sentinel agricultural and residential sites with HLC, sporozoite ELISA/PCR, and species-specific 18S rRNA detection linked to land-use/irrigation layers will produce EIR maps that guide time- and space-specific interventions. <cite id="21998773-0">Entomological surveillance at sentinel and active foci sites, integrated with epidemiology, accelerates elimination</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">ABR/EIR heterogeneity supports scaling preventive measures to reduce exposure and parasitemia</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Molecular and sporozoite data across ecological zones provide a reproducible basis for risk mapping</cite>. 
- Policy alignment: Ghana’s shift to high-quality, spatially explicit surveillance dovetails with NMEP’s 2021–2025 strategy to reduce morbidity/mortality by 75% and emphasizes surveillance to inform decisions; building local capacity in entomology and mapping strengthens last-mile control. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana’s 2014–2020 plan targeted 75% morbidity/mortality reduction via scaling interventions, underpinned by surveillance</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">NMCPs globally lack capacity for vector surveillance; strategic planning and trained entomology staff are key bottlenecks</cite>.

What’s new and first-in-region for Western North
- Western North remains sparsely characterized for molecularly resolved vectors and integrated EIR mapping; your study can be one of the first to deploy species-specific PCR (COI/SDR) plus Plasmodium 18S rRNA detection in cocoa/agricultural and peri-urban settings to resolve cryptic species and quantify infection risks, directly addressing the NMEP call for precision surveillance. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana-wide molecular form distribution is known broadly, but local baselines in transitional mosaics remain gaps; baseline surveys and molecular ID are urgently needed where reliable data are lacking</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">Only a small fraction of NMCPs have sufficient surveillance capacity, underscoring the value of first-in-region molecular mapping to inform control</cite>. 
- Integrating geospatial EIR with agricultural/urban land-use layers will yield a replicable framework for farm-level LSM (e.g., ditch management, biological control) and community-level LLIN targeting, aligning with observed drivers of heterogeneity and outdoor exposure. <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Microgeographic variation in ABR/EIR supports site-specific scaling of preventive measures</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor and field transmission highlight the need to extend control beyond indoor settings using spatially explicit data</cite>.

Methodological recommendations to strengthen the study
- Sampling design:
  - Agricultural sites: Include cocoa farms with and without irrigation; sample field edge pools, ditch-fed depressions, container habitats (plastic sheets, wheel tracks), and drainage channels; perform HLC indoors/outdoors and early-evening/night biting; collect resting and aquatic samples for molecular ID. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated and peri-urban sites harbor the most larval habitats; drainage ditches are highly productive LSM targets</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor biting and residual transmission support outdoor sampling to capture field exposure</cite>.
  - Residential/peri-urban sites: Target clusters near refuse, construction sites, drainage outfalls; compare compound vs. backyard vs. village periphery; standardize HLC and indoor resting collection. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Domestic effluent-driven drainage ditches and anthropogenic containers dominate breeding near residences</cite>.
- Molecular assays:
  - Vector species: COI barcoding with species replacement diagnostic regions (SRD/SPMS) to distinguish An. gambiae s.l. forms; confirm with morphological traits. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Morphological and molecular ID are complementary for robust species assignment</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Distribution of molecular forms informs control efficiency; baseline surveys are needed</cite>.
  - Infection detection: Nested or qPCR targeting Plasmodium 18S rRNA on blood-fed females; quantify sporozoite prevalence and oocyst intensities; genotype Plasmodium species using species-specific markers. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">PCR-based sporozoite infection rates and blood-meal analysis provide infection and exposure metrics</cite>.
- EIR estimation and mapping:
  - Compute EIR using ABR (HLC/CO2-baited traps) × sporozoite rate × vectorial capacity; integrate with land-use/land-cover, slope/aspect, and agricultural practices; identify spatial clusters for farm- and community-level prioritization. <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">ABR/EIR heterogeneity across villages maps to micro-ecological features and supports scaling preventive measures</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Combining entomological and epidemiological data with spatial context guides elimination strategies</cite>.
- Resistance and insecticide planning:
  - Profile susceptibility of An. gambiae s.l. to agricultural and public health insecticides; avoid cross-resistance by separating LLIN/IRS insecticide families from crop protection where feasible; recommend targeted rotations and biological control to reduce selection pressure. <cite id="45dcaaa6-2">Agricultural insecticide use increases resistance risk to malaria control; evidence-based susceptibility testing is needed</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">LLIN/IRS efficiency depends on molecular forms and resistance; baseline resistance monitoring is essential</cite>.
- Data systems and governance:
  - Integrate DHIMS malaria case data with EIR and vector species outputs to evaluate equity and impact; use participatory mapping with farmers to validate habitat inventory; build capacity for data-driven advocacy and NMEP alignment. <cite id="21998773-4">High-quality surveillance and constant surveillance inform control strategies; geospatial risk mapping supports preventive efforts</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">Programmatic capacity gaps in entomology and surveillance require investments in training and systems</cite>.

Policy and programmatic fit
- Ghana’s 2014–2020 plan targeted 75% reduction in morbidity/mortality; the 2021 GTSM emphasizes high-quality surveillance to guide universal coverage of core interventions. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana’s plan scaled preventive interventions aiming for 75% reduction by 2020 with surveillance to inform policy</cite> <cite id="21998773-4">High-quality surveillance data are central to the Global Technical Strategy for malaria elimination</cite>. 
- Evidence from Ghana and SSA shows that entomological surveillance at sentinel and active foci sites, coupled with epidemiological data, is foundational for last-mile elimination; your approach directly operationalizes this with molecular tools in Western North’s transitional landscape. <cite id="21998773-0">Entomological surveillance at sentinel and active foci, integrated with epidemiology, accelerates elimination by informing evidence-based interventions</cite>. 
- Capacity constraints within NMCPs globally and surveillance gaps in Ghana underscore that building local entomology capacity and deploying targeted, repeatable molecular surveillance will be a durable asset for NMEP’s transition toward elimination. <cite id="21998773-2">Only 8% of NMCPs report sufficient vector surveillance capacity; strategic planning and trained entomologists are key bottlenecks</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Scaling preventive measures to reduce exposure is effective, but requires accurate mapping of heterogeneity</cite>.

Summary of how these references sharpen your proposal
- Burden and heterogeneity: Use updated Ghana burden and village-level EIR heterogeneity to justify spatially explicit surveillance and targeted control in Western North’s mosaic landscape. <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">ABR/EIR heterogeneity and year-round infectiousness in microhabitats</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-0">Forest–savanna mosaic and rainfall patterns create breeding and transmission conducive conditions</cite>.
- Land-use drivers: Cite peri-urban/irrigated agriculture and anthropogenic drainage as primary larval sources; emphasize farm- and community-level hotspots. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated farming and peri-urban sites have the highest larval habitat frequency; drainage ditches are the most productive</cite>.
- Molecular precision: Emphasize cryptic species resolution (COI/SDR) and Plasmodium 18S rRNA for EIR attribution; integrate with geospatial mapping for precision surveillance. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Molecular identification and sporozoite PCR across ecological zones</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Entomological data linked to epidemiology for operational decision-making</cite>.
- Targeted interventions: Justify LSM on cocoa farms (drainage modification, biological control), outdoor residual control, and LLIN/IRS prioritization near residential hotspots; include insecticide resistance risk management. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">LSM targets include drainage ditches and anthropogenic containers</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor vectors and residual transmission require outdoor-focused control</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-2">Agricultural insecticides risk resistance; integrated management is needed</cite>.
- Governance and sustainability: Align with NMEP’s surveillance-driven strategy and note capacity investment needs for data-driven programmatic decisions. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Surveillance-informed scaling of interventions to meet national targets</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">Global capacity gaps in vector surveillance demand strengthened NMCP systems</cite>.

Limitations and next steps
- Western North-specific baselines are limited in the retrieved literature; initiating with a pilot across 5–8 paired agricultural and residential sites will calibrate methods and reveal priority clusters. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Baseline surveys and molecular form mapping are needed in areas with insufficient reliable data</cite>.
- Outdoor sampling logistics and safety require planning; integrating CO2-baited traps and early-evening sampling can complement HLC while reducing exposure. <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor biting peaks and residual transmission necessitate adapted sampling and control beyond indoors</cite>.
- Insecticide management plans should include resistance surveillance tied to the molecular forms detected. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Intervention efficiency depends on molecular forms and resistance; monitoring should be built into the study</cite>.

Title: Spatial temporal distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes in different ecological zones of Ghana
Snippet: Vector control is a cornerstone for malaria management in Sub-Saharan Africa. Understanding the distribution dynamics and ecology of major malaria vectors is important for strengthening the current control efforts of national malaria control programmes. This project monitored the spatiotemporal distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes across different ecological zones of Ghana from 2017 to 2025. Anopheles mosquitoes were sampled from twelve sites across the three ecological zones of Ghana (Coastal, Forest and Sahel Savannah zones) using human landing catches and Prokopack aspirators. Title: Malaria transmission intensity and dynamics of clinical malaria incidence in a mountainous forest region of Ghana
Snippet: Background Malaria transmission is heterogeneous. Villages close to each other may have very different transmission characteristics. The presence and abundance of malaria vectors is governed by local ecology and microclimate. Knowledge of the dynamics of transmission is important for planning and evaluation of malaria control strategies. This study investigated the heterogeneity of malaria transmission in preparation for a vaccine trial and offers insights into dynamics of malaria incidence in the forest zone of Ghana. Methods Malaria transmission was assessed in four villages with different micro-ecological features in the forest zone of the Akwapim-Mampong Range in Ghana, water shed with rivers flowing north to Lake Volta in the south. Human landing catches (HLC) of mosquitoes were conducted and Plasmodium falciparum circumsporozoite rates were assessed by ELISA. Sporozoite prevalence, annual biting rates (ABR) and entomological inoculation rates (EIR) from the four study sites were compared with climatological and ecological data. Regression analysis was used to compare transmission data and blood parasite prevalence, parasite density (PD) and malaria episodes from children in the study area. Additionally we examined trends in confirmed clinical malaria incidence from 2005 -2012. Results In total 1307 Anopheles gambiae s.l. and 54 An. funestus females were caught by HLC from November 2003 to August 2005. Sporozoites in Anopheles vectors in four villages ranged from 4.0 to 10.2%, ABR from 371 to 1890 and EIR from 40 to 158. Linear regression on parasitological and clinical data of children from the villages revealed that the ABR significantly influenced the parasite density (PD) of P. falciparum. Conclusion Malaria transmission was intense and heterogeneous and corresponded to the micro-ecological differences. Malaria transmission in the early evening hours before people went to sleep was enough to sustain stable malaria. Scaling up preventive measures to reduce exposure to vectors will be effective in reducing parasitemia in children. Variations in transmission intensity must be considered when evaluating impact of control strategies and interventions such as the vaccine trials.
</snippet>

Snippet: The mosquito Anopheles gambiae sensu lato (s.l.) contains seven species, of which An. gambiae sensu stricto (s.s), An. arabiensis and An. melas are three of the major vectors of lymphatic filariasis (LF) and malaria caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, and Plasmodium falciparum respectively in West Africa [1,2]. Vector control is considered an important tool for diseases transmitted by mosquitoes and other insect vectors [8]. The current Ghana policy on vector control against Anopheles vectors prioritizes the use of insecticide treated materials and indoor residual spraying. However, the efficiency of these interventions will depend on information on the distribution and abundance of the main vectors, the specific molecular forms of An. gambiae s.s and the levels of insecticide resistance within them [9,10]. 

Studies on the distribution of the An. gambiae complex in Africa [9,11], highlighted gaps in our knowledge, and Coetzee and colleagues [9] further recommended an urgent need for baseline surveys on the distribution of these malaria vectors in areas where no reliable information exists. Title: Diversity in breeding sites and distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes in selected urban areas of southern Ghana
Snippet: Already, among all the tropical diseases, malaria is considered the most common and devastating especially in SSA. In Ghana, malaria transmission is an all-year round phenomenon with peaks in the rainy seasons, and accounts for between 30-40% of outpatient visits to health facilities each year [12][13][14]. In Accra, malaria constitutes 40% of outpatient visits in most health facilities [15,16], a higher figure compared to the national average. This study aims at determining habitat preference of Anopheles mosquitoes in Accra and Sekondi-Takoradi municipalities of Ghana. We characterized the breeding places of Anopheles mosquitoes by origin, including man-made or naturally occurring and whether temporary or permanent, in 21 randomly selected points. Natural habitats were considered as naturally occurring, and man-made habitats were those created by anthropogenic activities. Water bodies in which larvae were found at least once and which dried up at least once during the sampling period were classified as temporary. We also defined a permanent habitat as the one in which Anopheles larva were found at least once and contain water throughout the sampling period. Habitat diversity and the types of Anopheles mosquito breeding in these habitats were also studied. In light of the recent reclassification of the M and S molecular forms of An. gambiae (s.s.), as An. coluzzii and An. gambiae (s.s.), respectively, it was found necessary to determine their habitat preferences in urban settings.

Title: Larval habitat diversity, physicochemical characterization and their effect on the density of larval malaria vectors in the city of Accra, Ghana
Snippet: Investigating malaria vector breeding habitat types, habitat characteristics and Anopheles larval abundance in urban settings is an essential element of urban malaria control (9). This can help in the elimination of urban malaria through effective larval source management. The present study assessed the larval habitat types, characteristics and their effect on the density of Anopheles gambiae s.l. in Accra, Ghana. Twelve (12) different larval habitat types, including drainage ditches, car tyres, and puddles were found. Irrigated urban farming (IUF) and Peri-urban (PU) sites had the highest frequency of larval habitats in dry and rainy season respectively. Drainage ditches were the most abundant and most productive habitat type for Anopheles mosquito larvae. Anopheles coluzzii is the most dominating malaria vector species found. This study identi ed the invasive malaria vector, An. stephensi for the rst time in Ghana. 

The most abundant habitat type was drainage ditches which carried e uents from people's homes. Other habitats such as car tires, hoof-prints and puddles were usually formed during the rainy season. Most of the mosquito breeding sites encountered during the survey in the different site categories resulted from anthropogenic activities, and their characteristics were related to factors associated with urbanization and agriculture. This emphasizes the importance of human activities through land-use in the creation of Anopheles breeding habitats and the impact they have on malaria transmission. Similar observation was reported in Accra and Takoradi (12), and in Cape Coast (19), Ghana, highlighting that man-made breeding habitats were the most abundant. The presence of numerous drainage ditches functioning as breeding habitats may stem from inadequate sanitation practices and insu ciently regulated urban development by both public authorities and residents. This results in the obstruction of drainage systems, allowing water to accumulate for extended periods and creating suitable conditions for mosquito breeding. In contrast, other studies highlighted puddles as the predominant breeding grounds for Anopheles mosquitoes in urban settings (12)(20). 

Even though there was seasonal variation in larval habitat abundance with higher abundance recorded in the rainy season, breeding habitats were found throughout the dry and rainy seasons across all site categories.
</snippet>

Title: Bionomics of malaria vectors in Lao PDR, 2018–2020: entomological surveillance as a key tool for malaria elimination
Snippet: Background The Lao PDR National Strategic Plan for malaria control and elimination for year 2021–2025 emphasizes the importance of routine entomological surveillance being conducted in areas with high transmission and in active malaria foci in elimination targeted areas. The collection of entomological surveillance data that is closely linked to recent epidemiological data is crucial for improving impact, as it contributes to the evidence package that supports operational and strategic decision-making of national malaria programmes, as they accelerate their last mile of elimination. Methods The Center for Malariology Parasitology and Epidemiology (CMPE) entomology team conducted entomological surveillance activities at 13 sentinel sites in 8 provinces and at active transmission foci sites from 2018 to 2020. The techniques used for the mosquito collection were indoor and outdoor human landing collections (from houses and from cultivation areas) and cattle baited net trap collections. Results There were 5601 Anopheles mosquito females captured and identified throughout the study, on both human and cow bait. They represented 15 different species or species complexes. The primary malaria vectors as well as the secondary vectors were present in all collection sites in the south, indicating that people living in these rural areas with high malaria incidence are exposed to the vectors. The vectors were highly zoophilic, but they still bite humans throughout the night with a high peak of activity before midnight, both indoors and outdoors. Overall, 17% of the malaria vectors were collected indoors when the people are sleeping. This confirms the importance of bed net use during the night. Thirty-two percent of primary and secondary vectors were collected outdoors at times when people are usually awake and outdoors, which shows that people are exposed to potentially infectious mosquitoes and the importance of personal protection at these times. The findings showed that residual transmission may occur outdoors in the villages, and outside the villages in cultivation fields and forested areas. Epidemiological data showed that transmission was higher in surveillance sites which were targeted as part of a malaria response rather than sentinel sites. Conclusions Understanding where and how transmission is persisting, monitoring and mapping vector species distribution in areas with active transmission, monitoring biting trends, and designing evidence based and effective vector control interventions are critical to accelerating progress toward malaria elimination. In this context, the role of entomological surveillance combined with epidemiological data should be considered as a cornerstone in achieving malaria elimination.

Title: Capacity of National Malaria Control Programmes to implement vector surveillance: a global analysis
Snippet: Solving the problem of malaria requires a highly skilled workforce with robust infrastructure, financial backing and sound programme management coordinated by a strategic plan. Here, the capacity of National Malaria Control Programmes (NMCPs) was analysed to identify the strengths and weaknesses underpinning the implementation of vector surveillance and control activities by the core elements of programme capacity, being strategic frameworks, financing, human resources, logistics and infrastructure, and information systems. Across nearly every country surveyed, the vector surveillance programmes were hampered by a lack of capacity and capability. Only 8% of NMCPs reported having sufficient capacity to implement vector surveillance. In contrast, 57%, 56% and 28% of NMCPs had the capacity to implement long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), indoor residual spraying (IRS) and larval source management (LSM) activities, respectively. Largely underlying this was a lack of up-to-date strategic plans that prioritize vector surveillance and include frameworks for decision-making and action. Strategic planning and a lack of well-trained entomologists heavily hamper vector surveillance. Countries on the path to elimination generally had more operational/field staff compared to countries at the stage of control, and also were more likely to have an established system for staff training and capacity building. It is unlikely that controlling countries will make significant progress unless huge investments also go towards increasing the number and capacity of programmatic staff.

Out of 599 malaria deaths recorded in 2018, 327 (54.6%) were recorded among children under five years [2].

This attempt is aimed at prevention and control of malaria across the country. Despite the efforts made over the years towards the control of malaria countrywide, the number of cases remain high, hence the need for continuous malaria surveillance system. The malaria surveillance system was set up to systematically monitor trends of malaria in the population, rapidly detect unusual events and epidemics and to plan and set priorities for health policies and programmes. With the setup and running of the surveillance system, it is expected that periodic evaluation of the system is done to ensure its efficient operation and ultimately, improvement in the health status of populations. Ghana adopted the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) guidelines in 2002, and data on priority diseases are reported through the District Health Information Management System (DHIMS) since 2012. From 2014 to 2016, Adaklu district recorded a total of 26,889 cases of malaria. an average of 8,963 per each of these years. However, 10,987 malaria cases were recorded in 2017 alone, an excess of 2,024 over the previous averages [4]. This trend of events prompted interest regarding the operation of the malaria surveillance system in the district. We evaluated the malaria surveillance system to determine if it is meeting its objectives and also assessed the system's attributes and usefulness.

The strategy was updated in the year 2021 to reflect the lessons learned in the global malaria response between 2016 to 2020. It provides a comprehensive framework to guide nations in their efforts to fast-track progress towards elimination of malaria by emphasizing the need for universal coverage of core malaria interventions for all populations at risk. At the heart of the strategy is the utmost need to use high-quality surveillance data for decision-making [14]. The alignment of the timeframe of the vision of AIM and GTSM to that of the SDG underscores the need to address the problem of under-five malaria to ensure the realization of SDG goal 3. Nonetheless, under-five malaria continues to be a significant cause of childhood deaths in SSA which militates against the progress towards the achievement of the sustainable development Goal 3 target 2.1. 

In Ghana, despite several national policies and interventions (e.g. Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS), Child Health Policy 2007-2015 and National Health Insurance, 2014-2020 Ghana Strategic Plan for Malaria Control) [1,10,15] rollout to improve and promote health of children, the under-five malaria and its resultant under-five mortality rates remain high in the country. The focus of the 2014-2020 Ghana Strategic Plan for Malaria Control is to scale up preventive interventions to reduce the malaria morbidity and mortality burden by 75% by the year 2020 [16]. 

There is limited knowledge on localized geospatial distribution of under-five malaria risk and how certain environmental predictors could help explain geographical differences in under-five malaria risk in Ghana. Also, malaria burden is a continuous phenomenon that requires high-quality surveillance data and constant surveillance to inform malaria control strategies. 

This study, therefore, attempts to fill these gaps.

Expected spatial patterns across cocoa/agricultural vs. residential/peri-urban sites
- Agricultural interfaces: Irrigated and non-irrigated crop lands (cocoa, plantains/bananas) create numerous artificial and semi-natural larval habitats (ditches, field edge pools, tyre/utensil collections, puddles), attract high densities of An. gambiae s.l., and sustain outdoor biting and sporozoite-positive outdoor collection. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated urban farming and peri-urban sites had the highest frequency of larval habitats; drainage ditches most productive</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor and residual transmission occurs in cultivation fields; 32% of vectors collected outdoors at times people are awake</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">Proximity to plantain/banana plantations associated with higher incidence; leaf axils harbor larvae</cite>.

- Spatial targeting of LLINs and IRS: Sites with high EIR and anthropophilic, endophilic biting should receive priority LLIN distribution and, where feasible, focal IRS; outdoor exposure calls for additional personal protection and community-level interventions. <cite id="21998773-0">Indoors account for 17% of collection; 32% outdoors at times people are awake, underscoring need for nets and personal protection</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Residual transmission outdoors in cultivation and forests necessitates spatially targeted control beyond indoor measures</cite>.

- Precision surveillance framework: Sentinel agricultural and residential sites with HLC, sporozoite ELISA/PCR, and species-specific 18S rRNA detection linked to land-use/irrigation layers will produce EIR maps that guide time- and space-specific interventions. <cite id="21998773-0">Entomological surveillance at sentinel and active foci sites, integrated with epidemiology, accelerates elimination</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">ABR/EIR heterogeneity supports scaling preventive measures to reduce exposure and parasitemia</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Molecular and sporozoite data across ecological zones provide a reproducible basis for risk mapping</cite>. 
- Policy alignment: Ghana’s shift to high-quality, spatially explicit surveillance dovetails with NMEP’s 2021–2025 strategy to reduce morbidity/mortality by 75% and emphasizes surveillance to inform decisions; building local capacity in entomology and mapping strengthens last-mile control. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana’s 2014–2020 plan targeted 75% morbidity/mortality reduction via scaling interventions, underpinned by surveillance</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">NMCPs globally lack capacity for vector surveillance; strategic planning and trained entomology staff are key bottlenecks</cite>.

- Western North remains sparsely characterized for molecularly resolved vectors and integrated EIR mapping; your study can be one of the first to deploy species-specific PCR (COI/SDR) plus Plasmodium 18S rRNA detection in cocoa/agricultural and peri-urban settings to resolve cryptic species and quantify infection risks, directly addressing the NMEP call for precision surveillance. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana-wide molecular form distribution is known broadly, but local baselines in transitional mosaics remain gaps; baseline surveys and molecular ID are urgently needed where reliable data are lacking</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">Only a small fraction of NMCPs have sufficient surveillance capacity, underscoring the value of first-in-region molecular mapping to inform control</cite>.

Methodological recommendations to strengthen the study
- Sampling design:
  - Agricultural sites: Include cocoa farms with and without irrigation; sample field edge pools, ditch-fed depressions, container habitats (plastic sheets, wheel tracks), and drainage channels; perform HLC indoors/outdoors and early-evening/night biting; collect resting and aquatic samples for molecular ID. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated and peri-urban sites harbor the most larval habitats; drainage ditches are highly productive LSM targets</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor biting and residual transmission support outdoor sampling to capture field exposure</cite>.
  - Residential/peri-urban sites: Target clusters near refuse, construction sites, drainage outfalls; compare compound vs. backyard vs. village periphery; standardize HLC and indoor resting collection. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Domestic effluent-driven drainage ditches and anthropogenic containers dominate breeding near residences</cite>.
- Molecular assays:
  - Vector species: COI barcoding with species replacement diagnostic regions (SRD/SPMS) to distinguish An. gambiae s.l. forms; confirm with morphological traits. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Morphological and molecular ID are complementary for robust species assignment</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Distribution of molecular forms informs control efficiency; baseline surveys are needed</cite>.
  - Infection detection: Nested or qPCR targeting Plasmodium 18S rRNA on blood-fed females; quantify sporozoite prevalence and oocyst intensities; genotype Plasmodium species using species-specific markers. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">PCR-based sporozoite infection rates and blood-meal analysis provide infection and exposure metrics</cite>.
- EIR estimation and mapping:
  - Compute EIR using ABR (HLC/CO2-baited traps) × sporozoite rate × vectorial capacity; integrate with land-use/land-cover, slope/aspect, and agricultural practices; identify spatial clusters for farm- and community-level prioritization. <cite id="45dcaaa6-3">ABR/EIR heterogeneity across villages maps to micro-ecological features and supports scaling preventive measures</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Combining entomological and epidemiological data with spatial context guides elimination strategies</cite>.
- Resistance and insecticide planning:
  - Profile susceptibility of An. gambiae s.l. to agricultural and public health insecticides; avoid cross-resistance by separating LLIN/IRS insecticide families from crop protection where feasible; recommend targeted rotations and biological control to reduce selection pressure. <cite id="45dcaaa6-2">Agricultural insecticide use increases resistance risk to malaria control; evidence-based susceptibility testing is needed</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">LLIN/IRS efficiency depends on molecular forms and resistance; baseline resistance monitoring is essential</cite>.
- Data systems and governance:
  - Integrate DHIMS malaria case data with EIR and vector species outputs to evaluate equity and impact; use participatory mapping with farmers to validate habitat inventory; build capacity for data-driven advocacy and NMEP alignment. <cite id="21998773-4">High-quality surveillance and constant surveillance inform control strategies; geospatial risk mapping supports preventive efforts</cite> <cite id="21998773-2">Programmatic capacity gaps in entomology and surveillance require investments in training and systems</cite>.

- Ghana’s 2014–2020 plan targeted 75% reduction in morbidity/mortality; the 2021 GTSM emphasizes high-quality surveillance to guide universal coverage of core interventions. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Ghana’s plan scaled preventive interventions aiming for 75% reduction by 2020 with surveillance to inform policy</cite> <cite id="21998773-4">High-quality surveillance data are central to the Global Technical Strategy for malaria elimination</cite>.

- Land-use drivers: Cite peri-urban/irrigated agriculture and anthropogenic drainage as primary larval sources; emphasize farm- and community-level hotspots. <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Irrigated farming and peri-urban sites have the highest larval habitat frequency; drainage ditches are the most productive</cite>.
- Molecular precision: Emphasize cryptic species resolution (COI/SDR) and Plasmodium 18S rRNA for EIR attribution; integrate with geospatial mapping for precision surveillance. <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Molecular identification and sporozoite PCR across ecological zones</cite> <cite id="21998773-0">Entomological data linked to epidemiology for operational decision-making</cite>.

- Outdoor sampling logistics and safety require planning; integrating CO2-baited traps and early-evening sampling can complement HLC while reducing exposure. <cite id="21998773-0">Outdoor biting peaks and residual transmission necessitate adapted sampling and control beyond indoors</cite>.
- Insecticide management plans should include resistance surveillance tied to the molecular forms detected. <cite id="45dcaaa6-4">Intervention efficiency depends on molecular forms and resistance; monitoring should be built into the study</cite>.

In sum, your proposal aligns with national and global shifts toward precision, surveillance-driven elimination and provides an opportunity to generate one of the first molecularly resolved, EIR-mapped profiles of malaria vectors in Western North Ghana’s agricultural–residential mosaics, directly informing targeted, land-use-aware control strategies. <cite id="21998773-0">Entomological surveillance integrated with epidemiology is foundational for last-mile elimination</cite> <cite id="45dcaaa6-1">Molecular species ID and sporozoite PCR across ecological zones provide actionable data for risk mapping</cite> <cite id="1c5ac6f5-1">Peri-urban and irrigated farming habitats concentrate larval sources, justifying farm-level LSM and surveillance</cite>.

Title: Assessing the prevalence, risk factors, and socio-demographic predictors of malaria among pregnant women in the Bono East Region of Ghana: a multicentre hospital-based mixed-method cross-sectional study
Snippet: The study was conducted in seven health facilities in seven municipalities/districts (namely: Atebubu-Amantin Municipal, Kintampo South District, Kintampo North Municipal, Nkoranza South Municipal, Techiman Municipal, Pru East District, and Pru West District). These seven municipalities/districts were all within the Bono East Region. Projections from the 2020 population and housing census indicated a total of 1,203,400 people, occupying 22,952 km 2 piece of land in the middle of Ghana, with a population density of 48.75 per sq km [16]. The Bono East Region borders the Savannah Region to the north, the Bono Region to the west, the Ashanti Region to the south, and Volta Lake to the east. It is made up of eleven municipalities/districts, with Techiman as its capital [16]. The region is located within the forestsavannah transitional ecological zone in the middle belt of Ghana. It experiences a double rainfall pattern, averaging 1399.5 mm per year, with average monthly temperatures ranging between 22 °C and 33 °C [17]. The major rainfall season typically occurs from March to June, while the minor season spans from September to November. These periods correspond to two peaks in malaria transmission [18]. Likewise, the region has abundant land and vegetation cover (savannah, tropical forest, and mangrove and swampy areas) with several rivers and streams [17]. The abundant land and vegetation, combined with the rainfall pattern and warm temperatures, create convenient conditions for the breeding of female Anopheles mosquitoes, thereby increasing malaria transmission in the region [19]. The predominant mosquito vectors distributed throughout the region are Anopheles gambiae, Anopheles arabiensis, and Anopheles funestus [20].

Title: Spatial temporal distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes in different ecological zones of Ghana
Snippet: Vector control is a cornerstone for malaria management in Sub-Saharan Africa. Understanding the distribution dynamics and ecology of major malaria vectors is important for strengthening the current control efforts of national malaria control programmes. This project monitored the spatiotemporal distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes across different ecological zones of Ghana from 2017 to 2025. Anopheles mosquitoes were sampled from twelve sites across the three ecological zones of Ghana (Coastal, Forest and Sahel Savannah zones) using human landing catches and Prokopack aspirators. Mosquitoes were subjected to morphological and molecular species identification. Sporozoite infection rates and blood meal sources of collected blood fed female mosquitoes were both assessed using PCR. A total of 47,771 Anopheline mosquitoes (An. gambiae s.l, An. funestus, An. pharoensis and An. rufipes) were collected across the three ecological zones. Anopheles gambiae s.l, and particularly An. coluzzii and An. gambiae s.s were the predominant species across the study sites and ecological zones. Sporozoite infections were higher in the forest and sahel zones compared to the coastal zone, and the overall human blood index was 40.46%. Our findings provide relevant data for improving current vector control for malaria in Ghana.

Title: Susceptibility of Anopheles Mosquito to Agricultural Insecticides in the Adansi North District, Ghana
Snippet: The New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD) in 2013 reported that there has been an increased utilisation of agricultural insecticides and has resulted in major reduction in harvest losses. Insecticides move through the environment; thus, the use of insecticides to control pests in agriculture has become a threat to malaria vector control (Diabate et al. 2002). The continuous utilisation of these chemicals is detrimental to humans and other life forms. There is also the risk of insecticide resistance which will lead to widespread failure of public health interventions. 

Agriculture is the backbone of Ghana's economy. It accounts for 29.9% of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of Ghana (Ghana Statistical Service 2010). Recent studies on the continuous use of insecticides in food production in the country to increase productivity and maximise profit has been reported (Elvis Asare 2015; Denkyirah et al. 2016). Hence there is the need for an evidence-based study to evaluate the susceptibility of the malaria vector to families of chemical insecticides utilised in malaria control interventions and in agriculture. This study sought to determine the susceptibility of Anopheles mosquito to some agricultural insecticides which are also used in public health for the control of mosquitoes at the Adansi north district, in the Ashanti Region of Ghana.

Title: Malaria transmission intensity and dynamics of clinical malaria incidence in a mountainous forest region of Ghana
Snippet: Background Malaria transmission is heterogeneous. Villages close to each other may have very different transmission characteristics. The presence and abundance of malaria vectors is governed by local ecology and microclimate. Knowledge of the dynamics of transmission is important for planning and evaluation of malaria control strategies. This study investigated the heterogeneity of malaria transmission in preparation for a vaccine trial and offers insights into dynamics of malaria incidence in the forest zone of Ghana. Methods Malaria transmission was assessed in four villages with different micro-ecological features in the forest zone of the Akwapim-Mampong Range in Ghana, water shed with rivers flowing north to Lake Volta in the south. Human landing catches (HLC) of mosquitoes were conducted and Plasmodium falciparum circumsporozoite rates were assessed by ELISA. Sporozoite prevalence, annual biting rates (ABR) and entomological inoculation rates (EIR) from the four study sites were compared with climatological and ecological data. Regression analysis was used to compare transmission data and blood parasite prevalence, parasite density (PD) and malaria episodes from children in the study area. Additionally we examined trends in confirmed clinical malaria incidence from 2005 -2012. Results In total 1307 Anopheles gambiae s.l. and 54 An. funestus females were caught by HLC from November 2003 to August 2005. Sporozoites in Anopheles vectors in four villages ranged from 4.0 to 10.2%, ABR from 371 to 1890 and EIR from 40 to 158. Linear regression on parasitological and clinical data of children from the villages revealed that the ABR significantly influenced the parasite density (PD) of P. falciparum. Conclusion Malaria transmission was intense and heterogeneous and corresponded to the micro-ecological differences. Malaria transmission in the early evening hours before people went to sleep was enough to sustain stable malaria. Scaling up preventive measures to reduce exposure to vectors will be effective in reducing parasitemia in children. Variations in transmission intensity must be considered when evaluating impact of control strategies and interventions such as the vaccine trials.

Title: Environmental Factors Associated with the Distribution of Anopheles gambiae s.s in Ghana; an Important Vector of Lymphatic Filariasis and Malaria
Snippet: The mosquito Anopheles gambiae sensu lato (s.l.) contains seven species, of which An. gambiae sensu stricto (s.s), An. arabiensis and An. melas are three of the major vectors of lymphatic filariasis (LF) and malaria caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, and Plasmodium falciparum respectively in West Africa [1,2]. In Ghana, previous studies have found the An. gambiae s.l and the An. funestus to be the major vectors of LF in the southern coastal zone and in the northern region of the country [3][4][5][6][7]. 

Vector control is considered an important tool for diseases transmitted by mosquitoes and other insect vectors [8]. The current Ghana policy on vector control against Anopheles vectors prioritizes the use of insecticide treated materials and indoor residual spraying. However, the efficiency of these interventions will depend on information on the distribution and abundance of the main vectors, the specific molecular forms of An. gambiae s.s and the levels of insecticide resistance within them [9,10]. 

Studies on the distribution of the An. gambiae complex in Africa [9,11], highlighted gaps in our knowledge, and Coetzee and colleagues [9] further recommended an urgent need for baseline surveys on the distribution of these malaria vectors in areas where no reliable information exists. Ghana is one of these countries. The largest and most recent study published on the abundance, distribution and levels of insecticide resistance in An. gambiae s.s covered 11 sites across different ecological zones of the country [12]. This study found that the An. gambiae S form predominated across the country, except in the arid north where only the M form was found. While this was the first major attempt at presenting the geographical distribution and ecological variations in An. gambiae s.s in Ghana, it is not known how these data compare with other An. gambiae s.s data, whether there are specific environmental factors driving the distributions of the M and S molecular forms, and if there are any associations with LF and malaria distributions [13,14].

documents.snippet: The study was conducted in seven health facilities in seven municipalities/districts (namely: Atebubu-Amantin Municipal, Kintampo South District, Kintampo North Municipal, Nkoranza South Municipal, Techiman Municipal, Pru East District, and Pru West District). These seven municipalities/districts were all within the Bono East Region. Projections from the 2020 population and housing census indicated a total of 1,203,400 people, occupying 22,952 km 2 piece of land in the middle of Ghana, with a population density of 48.75 per sq km [16]. The Bono East Region borders the Savannah Region to the north, the Bono Region to the west, the Ashanti Region to the south, and Volta Lake to the east. It is made up of eleven municipalities/districts, with Techiman as its capital [16]. The region is located within the forestsavannah transitional ecological zone in the middle belt of Ghana. It experiences a double rainfall pattern, averaging 1399.5 mm per year, with average monthly temperatures ranging between 22 °C and 33 °C [17]. The major rainfall season typically occurs from March to June, while the minor season spans from September to November. These periods correspond to two peaks in malaria transmission [18]. Likewise, the region has abundant land and vegetation cover (savannah, tropical forest, and mangrove and swampy areas) with several rivers and streams [17]. The abundant land and vegetation, combined with the rainfall pattern and warm temperatures, create convenient conditions for the breeding of female Anopheles mosquitoes, thereby increasing malaria transmission in the region [19]. documents.title: Spatial temporal distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes in different ecological zones of Ghana
documents.snippet: Vector control is a cornerstone for malaria management in Sub-Saharan Africa. Understanding the distribution dynamics and ecology of major malaria vectors is important for strengthening the current control efforts of national malaria control programmes. This project monitored the spatiotemporal distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes across different ecological zones of Ghana from 2017 to 2025. Anopheles mosquitoes were sampled from twelve sites across the three ecological zones of Ghana (Coastal, Forest and Sahel Savannah zones) using human landing catches and Prokopack aspirators. Mosquitoes were subjected to morphological and molecular species identification. Sporozoite infection rates and blood meal sources of collected blood fed female mosquitoes were both assessed using PCR. A total of 47,771 Anopheline mosquitoes (An. gambiae s.l, An. funestus, An. pharoensis and An. rufipes) were collected across the three ecological zones. Anopheles gambiae s.l, and particularly An. coluzzii and An. gambiae s.s were the predominant species across the study sites and ecological zones. Sporozoite infections were higher in the forest and sahel zones compared to the coastal zone, and the overall human blood index was 40.46%. Our findings provide relevant data for improving current vector control for malaria in Ghana.

Title: Diversity in breeding sites and distribution of Anopheles mosquitoes in selected urban areas of southern Ghana
Snippet: Already, among all the tropical diseases, malaria is considered the most common and devastating especially in SSA. Title: Larval habitat diversity, physicochemical characterization and their effect on the density of larval malaria vectors in the city of Accra, Ghana
Snippet: Investigating malaria vector breeding habitat types, habitat characteristics and Anopheles larval abundance in urban settings is an essential element of urban malaria control (9). This can help in the elimination of urban malaria through effective larval source management. The present study assessed the larval habitat types, characteristics and their effect on the density of Anopheles gambiae s.l. in Accra, Ghana. Twelve (12) different larval habitat types, including drainage ditches, car tyres, and puddles were found. Irrigated urban farming (IUF) and Peri-urban (PU) sites had the highest frequency of larval habitats in dry and rainy season respectively. Drainage ditches were the most abundant and most productive habitat type for Anopheles mosquito larvae. Anopheles coluzzii is the most dominating malaria vector species found. This study identi ed the invasive malaria vector, An. stephensi for the rst time in Ghana. 

The most abundant habitat type was drainage ditches which carried e uents from people's homes. Other habitats such as car tires, hoof-prints and puddles were usually formed during the rainy season. Most of the mosquito breeding sites encountered during the survey in the different site categories resulted from anthropogenic activities, and their characteristics were related to factors associated with urbanization and agriculture. This emphasizes the importance of human activities through land-use in the creation of Anopheles breeding habitats and the impact they have on malaria transmission. Similar observation was reported in Accra and Takoradi (12), and in Cape Coast (19), Ghana, highlighting that man-made breeding habitats were the most abundant. The presence of numerous drainage ditches functioning as breeding habitats may stem from inadequate sanitation practices and insu ciently regulated urban development by both public authorities and residents. This results in the obstruction of drainage systems, allowing water to accumulate for extended periods and creating suitable conditions for mosquito breeding. In contrast, other studies highlighted puddles as the predominant breeding grounds for Anopheles mosquitoes in urban settings (12)(20). 

Even though there was seasonal variation in larval habitat abundance with higher abundance recorded in the rainy season, breeding habitats were found throughout the dry and rainy seasons across all site categories.

Title: Bionomics of malaria vectors in Lao PDR, 2018–2020: entomological surveillance as a key tool for malaria elimination
Snippet: Background The Lao PDR National Strategic Plan for malaria control and elimination for year 2021–2025 emphasizes the importance of routine entomological surveillance being conducted in areas with high transmission and in active malaria foci in elimination targeted areas. The collection of entomological surveillance data that is closely linked to recent epidemiological data is crucial for improving impact, as it contributes to the evidence package that supports operational and strategic decision-making of national malaria programmes, as they accelerate their last mile of elimination. Methods The Center for Malariology Parasitology and Epidemiology (CMPE) entomology team conducted entomological surveillance activities at 13 sentinel sites in 8 provinces and at active transmission foci sites from 2018 to 2020. The techniques used for the mosquito collection were indoor and outdoor human landing collections (from houses and from cultivation areas) and cattle baited net trap collections. Results There were 5601 Anopheles mosquito females captured and identified throughout the study, on both human and cow bait. They represented 15 different species or species complexes. The primary malaria vectors as well as the secondary vectors were present in all collection sites in the south, indicating that people living in these rural areas with high malaria incidence are exposed to the vectors. The vectors were highly zoophilic, but they still bite humans throughout the night with a high peak of activity before midnight, both indoors and outdoors. Overall, 17% of the malaria vectors were collected indoors when the people are sleeping. This confirms the importance of bed net use during the night. Thirty-two percent of primary and secondary vectors were collected outdoors at times when people are usually awake and outdoors, which shows that people are exposed to potentially infectious mosquitoes and the importance of personal protection at these times. The findings showed that residual transmission may occur outdoors in the villages, and outside the villages in cultivation fields and forested areas. Epidemiological data showed that transmission was higher in surveillance sites which were targeted as part of a malaria response rather than sentinel sites. Conclusions Understanding where and how transmission is persisting, monitoring and mapping vector species distribution in areas with active transmission, monitoring biting trends, and designing evidence based and effective vector control interventions are critical to accelerating progress toward malaria elimination. In this context, the role of entomological surveillance combined with epidemiological data should be considered as a cornerstone in achieving malaria elimination.

Title: Capacity of National Malaria Control Programmes to implement vector surveillance: a global analysis
Snippet: Solving the problem of malaria requires a highly skilled workforce with robust infrastructure, financial backing and sound programme management coordinated by a strategic plan. Here, the capacity of National Malaria Control Programmes (NMCPs) was analysed to identify the strengths and weaknesses underpinning the implementation of vector surveillance and control activities by the core elements of programme capacity, being strategic frameworks, financing, human resources, logistics and infrastructure, and information systems. Across nearly every country surveyed, the vector surveillance programmes were hampered by a lack of capacity and capability. Only 8% of NMCPs reported having sufficient capacity to implement vector surveillance. In contrast, 57%, 56% and 28% of NMCPs had the capacity to implement long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), indoor residual spraying (IRS) and larval source management (LSM) activities, respectively. Largely underlying this was a lack of up-to-date strategic plans that prioritize vector surveillance and include frameworks for decision-making and action. Strategic planning and a lack of well-trained entomologists heavily hamper vector surveillance. Countries on the path to elimination generally had more operational/field staff compared to countries at the stage of control, and also were more likely to have an established system for staff training and capacity building. It is unlikely that controlling countries will make significant progress unless huge investments also go towards increasing the number and capacity of programmatic staff.

Title: Mapping under-five child malaria risk that accounts for environmental and climatic factors to aid malaria preventive and control efforts in Ghana: Bayesian geospatial and interactive web-based mapping methods
Snippet: In May 2015, the Global technical strategy for malaria (GTSM) 2016-2030 which sets the target of reducing global malaria incidence and mortality rates by at least 90% by 2030 was adopted by the World Health Assembly. There is limited knowledge on localized geospatial distribution of under-five malaria risk and how certain environmental predictors could help explain geographical differences in under-five malaria risk in Ghana. Also, malaria burden is a continuous phenomenon that requires high-quality surveillance data and constant surveillance to inform malaria control strategies. 

This study, therefore, attempts to fill these gaps.

documents.snippet:
In May 2015, the Global technical strategy for malaria (GTSM) 2016-2030 which sets the target of reducing global malaria incidence and mortality rates by at least 90% by 2030 was adopted by the World Health Assembly. The strategy was updated in the year 2021 to reflect the lessons learned in the global malaria response between 2016 to 2020. It provides a comprehensive framework to guide nations in their efforts to fast-track progress towards elimination of malaria by emphasizing the need for universal coverage of core malaria interventions for all populations at risk. At the heart of the strategy is the utmost need to use high-quality surveillance data for decision-making [14]. The alignment of the timeframe of the vision of AIM and GTSM to that of the SDG underscores the need to address the problem of under-five malaria to ensure the realization of SDG goal 3. Nonetheless, under-five malaria continues to be a significant cause of childhood deaths in SSA which militates against the progress towards the achievement of the sustainable development Goal 3 target 2.1. 

In Ghana, despite several national policies and interventions (e.g. Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS), Child Health Policy 2007-2015 and National Health Insurance, 2014-2020 Ghana Strategic Plan for Malaria Control) [1,10,15] rollout to improve and promote health of children, the under-five malaria and its resultant under-five mortality rates remain high in the country. The focus of the 2014-2020 Ghana Strategic Plan for Malaria Control is to scale up preventive interventions to reduce the malaria morbidity and mortality burden by 75% by the year 2020 [16]. 

There is limited knowledge on localized geospatial distribution of under-five malaria risk and how certain environmental predictors could help explain geographical differences in under-five malaria risk in Ghana. Also, malaria burden is a continuous phenomenon that requires high-quality surveillance data and constant surveillance to inform malaria control strategies. 

This study, therefore, attempts to fill these gaps.
